title: Python for Data Analysis
description: Learn Python tools and programming techniques commonly used in data analysis workflows.
objectives: Set up an isolated project environment with venv and install packages into it.
Work fluently in Jupyter Notebook — cells, run order, and restart.
Replace simple loops with list comprehensions.
Use lambda with map(), filter(), and zip() to transform data.

slides.title: Python for Data Analysis
slides.lead: Two things separate a script writer from an analyst: a clean environment to work in, and the compact syntax that data code is written in.
bullets: Jupyter Notebook — where analysis actually happens
Virtual environments — keeping projects from breaking each other
Comprehensions — loops in one line
lambda, map, filter, zip — the functional toolkit

slides.title: Why notebooks for data work
slides.lead: A notebook mixes code, output, and explanation in one document, and lets you re-run a single step without re-running everything.
bullets: Code cells run with Shift + Enter
The value of the last line in a cell is displayed automatically
Markdown cells hold your notes and headings
Charts and tables render inline, right under the code
The whole file (.ipynb) is shareable as a report

body: jupyter notebook          # opens in your browser

slides.title: Run order is the one real trap
slides.lead: Cells share one memory space and run in whatever order you click them — not top to bottom.
bullets: The [ ] number shows the order cells actually ran
A deleted cell's variables still exist in memory
Kernel ▸ Restart & Run All is the truth test
Do that before you share or submit any notebook
Shortcuts: Esc then A / B to add a cell, D D to delete, M for markdown
slides.note: "It worked before I restarted" means the notebook depended on a cell you already changed. Restart & Run All catches it every time.

slides.title: One environment per project
slides.lead: A virtual environment is a private folder of packages, so Project A on Pandas 1.5 cannot break Project B on Pandas 2.2.
bullets: Created inside the project folder, usually named .venv
Must be activated in each new terminal
pip install then writes into that folder only
Add .venv/ to .gitignore — never commit it
Share requirements.txt instead of the folder

body: pip install pandas numpy matplotlib jupyter

slides.title: Checking you are in the right one
slides.lead: Most "module not found" errors are really "installed into a different environment".

slides.title: A loop that builds a list, in one line
slides.lead: Read it as: the expression, for each item, optionally where a condition holds.
bullets: [expr for item in iterable]
[expr for item in iterable if condition]
Faster and shorter than append in a loop
Works for dicts too: {k: v for ...}
If it needs two conditions and a nested loop, use a normal loop instead

body: passed = [s for s in scores if s >= 50]

slides.title: Small anonymous functions
slides.lead: A lambda is a one-expression function with no name — used where a function is expected for a moment and never again.
bullets: lambda args: expression
The expression's value is returned automatically
No statements, no if blocks, no loops inside
Most common use: the key= argument of sorted()
If you need a name for it, use def instead

body: ranked = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s["score"], reverse=True)

slides.title: map() — apply a function to every item
slides.lead: map returns a lazy iterator, so wrap it in list() when you want to see or reuse the result.

slides.note: map(float, raw) is the clearest version — pass an existing function by name, no lambda needed.

slides.title: filter() — keep the items that pass a test
slides.lead: The function you pass must return True or False. Items returning True are kept.

body: # filter also drops empty / falsy values

slides.note: [s for s in scores if s >= 50] does the same job and most Python teams prefer it. Know both — you will read both.

slides.title: zip() — walk two lists side by side
slides.lead: zip pairs items by position and stops at the shortest list.

body: for name, score in zip(names, scores):

bullets: names = ["Sokha", "Dara", "Mony", "Vira"] and scores = ["87.5", "41", "73.5", "92"]
1. Convert scores to floats with map()
2. Build a list of dicts with zip() and a comprehension
